This study introduces a novel class of time-varying Poisson autoregressive models, termed TVPARCH(p,q), designed to capture both time-varying volatility and nonlinearity in count data. We establish the existence and uniqueness of the stationary solution for the TVPARCH(p,q) model and derive its first- and second-order moment properties. Furthermore, we propose a consistent estimation method based on a quasi-maximum likelihood approach and develop a testing procedure to determine the optimal order of the TVPARCH(p,q) model. The efficacy of these methods is demonstrated through simulations and an empirical analysis of daily newspaper article counts related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The findings indicate that the TVPARCH(p,q) model effectively captures the volatility clustering and nonlinearity inherent in the data. Additionally, the estimated time-varying parameters reveal that the impact of past information on current volatility is more pronounced during periods of high volatility.

This study introduces a novel technique for quantifying atmospheric aerosols by leveraging the photometric variability of stars. The method relies on the diffraction of starlight by aerosols, which induces a reduction in stellar flux. By analyzing the diffraction pattern through a Fourier transform, we can derive the aerosol's vertical optical depth. We validated this approach using data from the TESS mission, which monitored 1,000 stars over 1,000 days. The results show that the derived optical depths align well with those measured by AERONET, a network of ground-based sun photometers. Furthermore, we developed a new method to estimate the uncertainty of the retrieved optical depths. This technique involves creating a synthetic dataset of stars with known optical depths, applying our retrieval algorithm, and comparing the results against the actual values. We also examined the impact of stellar variability on the accuracy of the retrieved optical depths. Finally, we demonstrated that the new uncertainty estimation method is effective by applying it to the TESS dataset. This work presents a novel, independent technique for measuring atmospheric aerosols, which could be valuable for validating data from satellite sensors. The method is particularly useful for monitoring aerosols in regions lacking ground-based sun photometers, such as the Pacific Ocean, where TESS has observed numerous stars. Additionally, this approach could serve as an independent verification tool for future satellite missions, such as the planned PACE satellite, which will observe the Pacific Ocean. The method is applicable to any dataset where stellar variability is recorded over time, including data from ground-based telescopes. We anticipate that this technique will be valuable for future studies. The code used in this work is available at https://github.com/astromeghan/AerosolRetrieval.

This study introduces a novel, straightforward, and computationally efficient algorithm for sampling configurational distributions in molecular systems. The method integrates a deterministic, time-reversible, and symplectic integrator with a stochastic, time-reversible, and ergodic Langevin thermostat. We establish that this approach generates a Markov chain that converges to the target configurational distribution, with a convergence rate that is independent of the system's dimensionality. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asymptotic variance of Monte Carlo estimators for configurational averages remains constant regardless of the integration time step. Numerical experiments on Lennard-Jones fluids and TIP4P/2005 water confirm that the algorithm is both rapid and accurate, with the asymptotic variance of Monte Carlo estimators for configurational averages remaining stable across a wide range of time steps. These findings indicate that the method is highly effective for estimating configurational averages in systems where sampling is otherwise difficult, such as those exhibiting first-order phase transitions. The algorithm is implemented in the open-source package PLUMED2, which can be integrated with various molecular dynamics simulation codes. Additionally, we provide a simple, generic implementation in Python, available at https://github.com/huacnlee/ConfSample. The proposed algorithm is applicable to any molecular system for which a molecular dynamics integrator can be defined. This study examines the extent to which human reference data can serve as a reliable metric for assessing the quality of generated image descriptions. We introduce a new dataset comprising 1,000 image-text pairs, where each image is paired with two distinct human-written descriptions. Additionally, we incorporate descriptions from three state-of-the-art models: Flickr8k-Caption, MS-COCO-Reflexion, and T2I-Adapter. Our analysis reveals that the two human descriptions for a single image often differ significantly in content, leading to low BLEU scores for both when compared against the other. Consequently, relying solely on BLEU to evaluate automatic descriptions is problematic. We further demonstrate that the reference data used to train these models are not representative of the full dataset, causing the models to achieve inflated BLEU scores. Ultimately, we conclude that human reference data are unsuitable for evaluating image descriptions generated by models trained on large-scale datasets like Flickr8k and MS-COCO. Instead, we propose a new metric, the Image Description Quality (IDQ) score, which offers a more accurate assessment of generated descriptions. The IDQ score is derived from a BERT-based model trained on a dataset of 1,000 image pairs, each containing one automatic description and one human-written description. We validate the IDQ metric by showing a strong correlation between its scores and human evaluations of description quality. The IDQ metric and the associated dataset are available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/ImageDescriptionQualityMetric.

We introduce a novel method for calculating quantum complexity in free conformal field theories (CFTs) by leveraging the Euler-Arnold equation. This approach yields a closed-form expression for the complexity of Gaussian states, which we term the Euler-Arnold complexity. We demonstrate that this measure aligns with the geodesic distance on the space of Gaussian states when equipped with the Maassen-Uffink (M-U) inner product. Furthermore, we establish that the Euler-Arnold complexity satisfies the triangle inequality, confirming its validity as a metric. As a practical application, we derive a closed-form formula for the complexity growth between vacuum and thermal states in 2D free CFTs. Our results indicate that the Euler-Arnold complexity grows linearly with time for short durations, mirroring the behavior of geodesic complexity. However, for longer times, the growth rate of the Euler-Arnold complexity exceeds that of the geodesic complexity. We conclude by discussing the implications of these findings. The derivation of a closed-form expression for the geodesic complexity of 2D free CFTs relies on the existence of a specific conformal embedding into a 3D free scalar field theory, a technique we also detail. Finally, we extend the definition of Euler-Arnold complexity to general $d$-dimensional free CFTs and derive a closed-form formula for the geodesic complexity in 4D free CFTs. These results suggest that a similar closed-form expression for geodesic complexity in arbitrary $d$-dimensional free CFTs is feasible. Our findings suggest that the Euler-Arnold complexity could serve as a valuable tool for investigating quantum complexity in various physical systems. The connection between the Euler-Arnold equation and quantum complexity may offer new insights into the relationship between complexity and geometry in quantum field theories. Additionally, the concept of Euler-Arnold complexity could potentially be applied to other areas of physics, such as general relativity. We anticipate that this work will stimulate further research into the interplay between the Euler-Arnold equation and quantum complexity. Fitting parton distribution functions (PDFs) to experimental data is a non-perturbative inverse problem that requires solving a complex integral equation. This process relies on a theoretical pipeline to convert parton-level predictions into hadron-level predictions, which are then compared with data. While existing pipelines have been developed for specific fitting groups, they are often ad hoc and lack the modularity needed for a universal solution. To address this, we introduce a modular, extensible, and open-source Python-based pipeline designed for PDF fitting. This pipeline integrates the fastxsection module, which calculates parton-level cross sections, with a novel framework for performing the convolution integral. We validate the pipeline by reproducing results from established PDF sets and by generating new predictions for processes not yet included in standard sets. Furthermore, we demonstrate the pipeline's utility by fitting a new set of PDFs to a comprehensive collection of LHC data. The resulting set, named CT14, is available at http://www.lapp.infn.it/cteq/ct14.html. The source code for this project can be accessed at https://github.com/CTEQ-Steering-Group/theory_pipeline_for_pdf_fitting. This work represents a significant step toward a universal, modular, and extensible pipeline for PDF fitting, which will be essential for future global fits incorporating data from the High-Luminosity LHC. The pipeline will also support the fitting of parton shower functions and other non-perturbative functions, such as fragmentation functions and intrinsic transverse momentum distributions. Additionally, it will enable the fitting of PDFs for exotic hadrons, including tetraquarks and pentaquarks, and facilitate the calculation of cross sections for rare processes at the LHC. Ultimately, this universal pipeline will serve as a valuable tool for the broader high-energy physics community. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license.

This study employs a linearized framework to model the response of a turbulent jet flame to acoustic forcing, utilizing a novel active flame approach. The model incorporates a linearized description of the turbulent flow field, which is driven by acoustic perturbations and superimposed on a base flow generated by a jet velocity. This linearized flow description is integrated into a linearized flame model, which is subsequently coupled with a linearized acoustic model to form a comprehensive system. The resulting model is validated against direct numerical simulation (DNS) data, demonstrating strong agreement in predicting the flame's response to acoustic perturbations. Furthermore, the model's ability to forecast the flame's reaction to simultaneous acoustic and jet velocity perturbations is examined. The findings indicate that the flame's response to acoustic perturbations is significantly influenced by the jet velocity perturbations, a phenomenon that aligns with DNS results. Additionally, the model reveals that the flame's response to acoustic perturbations is sensitive to the spatial distribution of jet velocity perturbations, a characteristic also confirmed by DNS. These results suggest that the proposed model can effectively predict the flame's response to acoustic perturbations within a range of jet velocity perturbations, provided the linearized flow description remains valid. Ultimately, this model offers a valuable tool for investigating the impact of jet velocity perturbations on the flame's response to acoustic perturbations, thereby aiding in the development of active control strategies for turbulent jet flames. The model is accessible at https://github.com/Aditya-1999/Linearized_Turbulent_Jet_Flame.

This study introduces a nonlocal extension of Einstein-Cartan gravity, termed nonlocal gravity, which incorporates a nonlocal spin-torsion interaction. We formulate a nonlocal generalization of the Frenkel spin constraint and derive the corresponding nonlocal constitutive relation for torsion. Furthermore, we establish a nonlocal version of the Cartan constitutive relation, which links torsion to curvature. By deriving the nonlocal field equations, we demonstrate that the nonlocal generalization of the Frenkel constraint is not required to eliminate the nonlocal spin-torsion term from the gravitational action. Consequently, the nonlocal constitutive relation for torsion can be defined without relying on the Frenkel constraint. We also derive the nonlocal generalization of the Einstein-Cartan constitutive relation, which connects curvature to spin. Finally, we derive the nonlocal generalization of the Einstein-Weiss constitutive relation, which relates curvature to both spin and torsion. These constitutive relations are essential for formulating the nonlocal gravitational constitutive tensor, which serves as the foundation for the constitutive approach to nonlocal gravity. The derivation of these nonlocal generalizations relies on a nonlocal extension of the Cartan connection, which we also present. Additionally, we introduce a nonlocal generalization of the fundamental tetrad, which is necessary for defining the nonlocal gravitational energy-momentum tensor. We conclude by deriving the nonlocal gravitational constitutive tensor and the associated nonlocal gravitational constitutive tensor potential. This work represents the first attempt to derive the constitutive tensor for nonlocal gravity. The LHC is renowned for creating high-multiplicity events, yet it also generates low-multiplicity events that are valuable for studying rare processes and small systems. These low-multiplicity events are particularly significant for investigating the onset of collective phenomena in small systems, such as the formation of a quark-gluon plasma. This paper provides an overview of low-multiplicity events at the LHC, with a specific focus on the ALICE experiment. We examine the characteristics of these events, the associated challenges, and the strategies employed to address them. Furthermore, we highlight the unique features of low-multiplicity events at the LHC compared to those at RHIC and discuss the prospects for studying small systems at future colliders. Finally, we summarize the results from low-multiplicity events at the LHC, emphasizing the evidence for collective behavior in small systems. The findings indicate that the onset of collective phenomena occurs at a system size of approximately $N_{part}\sim 100$, which aligns with hydrodynamic predictions. Additionally, we discuss the potential for exploring the initial state in small systems through long-range azimuthal correlations, a phenomenon previously observed in high-multiplicity events. We also address the challenges in measuring this effect in low-multiplicity events and the strategies used to overcome them. Ultimately, we conclude that the onset of collective phenomena in small systems at the LHC coincides with the emergence of initial-state correlations, suggesting that both effects are driven by the same underlying physics. This conclusion is supported by the observation that the magnitude of initial-state correlations increases with system size, mirroring the behavior of collective phenomena. These results suggest that initial-state correlations are a consequence of the same physics responsible for collective phenomena, rather than a separate effect. This insight is crucial for understanding the physics governing small systems at the LHC. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 outlines the characteristics of low-multiplicity events at the LHC, the associated challenges, and the solutions implemented. Section 3 reviews the results on collective phenomena in small systems at the LHC. Section 4 discusses the prospects for studying initial-state correlations in low-multiplicity events at the LHC. Section 5 summarizes the findings on initial-state correlations in small systems at the LHC. Finally, Section 6 presents our conclusions.

Neutron star X-ray binaries in the Milky Way are categorized into two groups: persistent sources, which maintain a constant X-ray luminosity, and transient sources, which experience periodic outbursts. While the existence of persistent sources is straightforward, the origin of transients remains a subject of debate. This paper examines the connection between these two populations by analyzing the distribution of recurrence times for transient systems. We introduce a method to determine the minimum mass accretion rate required for a binary to sustain persistent accretion. Applying this approach to a sample of 14 transient systems, we find that the minimum accretion rate needed for persistence is approximately $10^{-9}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. Consequently, the 14 systems in our sample should have already transitioned to persistent behavior if their current mass accretion rates exceed this threshold. Our analysis indicates that the quiescent neutron star binaries in the Galactic Centre likely fall into this category. Furthermore, we propose that the transient nature of the 14 systems studied arises from stochastic variations in their mass accretion rates, which occasionally dip below the critical value of $10^{-9}$ M$_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$. This mechanism also offers a potential explanation for the transient behavior observed in the Galactic Centre. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the formation of neutron star X-ray binaries. The results presented here align with the conclusions of our companion paper by Fulsang et al. This study introduces HyperDegrade, a novel technique designed to extend the battery life of mobile devices by dynamically reducing CPU frequencies. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on coarse-grained frequency steps, HyperDegrade leverages a combination of hardware and software mechanisms to achieve fine-grained frequency reductions. These reductions are implemented without compromising system performance, ensuring that applications continue to run at their original speeds. The core of HyperDegrade involves a hardware-based method for lowering CPU frequencies and a software-based approach for managing the resulting performance degradation. We evaluated HyperDegrade on a smartphone running Android 10, demonstrating that it can achieve up to a 2.5x improvement in battery life compared to standard dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS) methods. Furthermore, the system can operate at effective frequencies as low as 1/10th of the CPU's maximum, delivering a 1.7x gain in battery life over existing battery-saving features. This study tackles the challenge of coordinating multiple tasks among a team of robots operating on a regular network, where each robot has restricted computational and communication resources. We introduce a novel, fully distributed algorithm that enables robots to select tasks and communicate using a simple, local, and asynchronous protocol. This approach requires minimal memory and computational power, along with a low communication rate. The algorithm is grounded in a strategic game-theoretic framework, where each robot acts as a rational agent aiming to maximize its own utility. We define a utility function that accounts for the time needed to complete tasks, the quality of service delivered, and the communication costs incurred. Our analysis demonstrates that the proposed algorithm converges to a Nash equilibrium, ensuring that the team collectively achieves high-quality service for all tasks. Simulation results confirm the algorithm's effectiveness and validate the theoretical findings. The proposed method is applicable to various scenarios, including disaster response, search and rescue operations, and environmental monitoring.

The sensitivity of current gravitational wave detectors at high frequencies is constrained by shot noise, a limitation that will persist even with future upgrades. To address this, we propose integrating sloshing-Sagnac interferometers into the output light path of high-frequency signal recycling configurations. This design functions as an optical amplifier, effectively lowering shot noise. We present a detailed analysis of the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer's response to gravitational waves and demonstrate that combining it with a Michelson interferometer creates a hybrid interferometer capable of surpassing the shot noise limit of conventional setups. Furthermore, we show that this hybrid configuration can achieve a flat sensitivity curve at high frequencies, potentially improving overall detector sensitivity. Our findings indicate that integrating a sloshing-Sagnac interferometer into a Michelson interferometer could enhance the sensitivity of Advanced LIGO by up to a factor of 1.6 between 1.5 and 2.5 kHz, and by a factor of 2.1 between 2.5 and 3.5 kHz. These results suggest that the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer is a viable solution for boosting high-frequency sensitivity in gravitational wave detectors. Extra-large-scale multiple-input multiple-output (XL-MIMO) systems are recognized for their remarkable ability to enhance spectral efficiency through massive array gains. However, these systems face significant challenges in implementing random access protocols due to the non-overlapping nature of their visibility regions. This paper investigates the non-overlapping visibility regions within an XL-MIMO random access protocol. We first derive the exact expression for the number of visible users at the access point (AP) and demonstrate that this count follows a Poisson distribution. Furthermore, we derive the exact formula for the probability of successful access and analyze how it relates to the non-overlapping visibility regions. Simulation results confirm the accuracy of our analytical findings and provide additional insights into the system's performance. Ultimately, we propose a novel random access protocol designed to maximize the probability of successful access. The analytical results indicate that this new protocol can increase the probability of successful access by up to 100% compared to the conventional XL-MIMO random access approach. These findings offer valuable guidance for optimizing XL-MIMO systems.

The results demonstrate that the remote LDV system achieves accuracy comparable to the hot-wire anemometer. Furthermore, the system's capability to capture 2D velocity data at various points was confirmed by generating a velocity vector map. This remote LDV system offers a cost-effective solution for obtaining 2D velocity data at multiple locations, making it a valuable tool for studying complex flow structures. Lack of annotated data remains a significant barrier to developing effective brain lesion segmentation models. To address this, we introduce a novel framework for synthesizing brain lesions using a Progressive Adversarial Variational Auto-Encoder (PAVAE). This approach integrates a Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE) with a Progressive GAN (PGAN) to generate realistic lesion images. The model operates in two stages: first, a VAE creates a coarse lesion map, which is then refined by a PGAN to produce a realistic final output. We evaluated the synthesized images using a FID metric and assessed the segmentation performance of a U-Net model trained on both real and synthetic data. Results indicate that the PAVAE-generated images are realistic, and incorporating them into training data significantly enhances the segmentation accuracy of the U-Net model. The proposed method offers a practical solution for creating synthetic brain lesion images, thereby improving the performance of supervised brain lesion segmentation models. The source code is available at https://github.com/Abhishek-1999/PAVAE.

Feature extraction serves as a fundamental technique for addressing various computer vision challenges, including image classification, detection, and segmentation. While numerous methods have been developed, they often lack a unified framework. This paper introduces a unified framework grounded in contrastive learning, which leverages the inherent characteristics of different vision tasks to derive task-specific features. We demonstrate that existing feature extraction approaches can be categorized into three categories: unsupervised, semi-supervised, and supervised. By integrating these methods with contrastive learning, we formulate a unified framework capable of deriving task-specific features. We validate the effectiveness of this framework across multiple vision tasks, showing that the resulting features significantly enhance performance in both traditional and emerging tasks. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach for image classification that surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The proposed framework is versatile and applicable to various vision tasks, offering a valuable resource for future research. Despite the rapid growth of large language models (LLMs), integrating structured knowledge remains a significant challenge. This issue is particularly acute for specialized domains, where the sheer volume of knowledge exceeds the capacity of current LLMs. To address this, we introduce SKILL, a framework that infuses structured knowledge into LLMs via a two-stage process: first, a knowledge graph is converted into a structured representation, and second, this representation is incorporated into the LLM's context window. We evaluate SKILL on three tasks: answering questions about structured knowledge, performing reasoning over such knowledge, and generating text grounded in structured knowledge. Our results demonstrate that SKILL significantly outperforms existing methods on all three tasks. Furthermore, we find that the performance of both SKILL and baseline approaches is closely tied to the size of the included knowledge graph. To support future research, we release a dataset containing 1.5 million triples from 11 knowledge graphs covering 11 specialized domains, along with a Python implementation of the SKILL framework. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/IBM/SKILL.

This study examines the connection between the shadow radius and the first-order phase transition of non-linear charged AdS black holes. The findings indicate that the shadow radius initially decreases and then increases as the charge grows. Furthermore, the shadow radius exhibits a non-monotonic dependence on temperature, reaching a minimum at the critical temperature. The relationship between the shadow radius and charge aligns with the behavior of the horizon radius, suggesting that the shadow radius can serve as an effective proxy for the horizon radius. Additionally, the shadow radius displays a non-monotonic variation with respect to the non-linear electrodynamics parameter, mirroring the trend observed in the horizon radius. These results suggest that the shadow radius is influenced by the non-linear electrodynamics parameter and can be utilized to investigate the thermodynamic properties of non-linear charged AdS black holes. The analysis of the shadow radius offers a novel approach for exploring the thermodynamics of non-linear charged AdS black holes. Quantum entanglement and synchronization represent two distinct non-classical phenomena that have garnered significant attention in recent years. This study introduces a novel method for detecting both entanglement and synchronization directly from Wigner-Weyl tomograms. We demonstrate that entanglement manifests as a sudden drop in the tomogram's value, whereas synchronization appears as a sharp peak. These findings are illustrated using the thermal states of two harmonic oscillators. Furthermore, we establish that the onset of synchronization coincides with the emergence of quantum entanglement. The proposed approach offers a straightforward and effective means of identifying entanglement and synchronization within Wigner-Weyl tomograms, potentially serving as a valuable tool for analyzing non-classical effects in other quantum systems. Ultimately, this work highlights the utility of Wigner-Weyl tomograms in uncovering non-classical phenomena. This paper investigates biharmonic hypersurfaces within Euclidean space that possess recurrent shape, Ricci, or semi-symmetric tensor operators. We establish that a biharmonic hypersurface in Euclidean space with a recurrent shape operator must be totally umbilical. Furthermore, we prove that a biharmonic hypersurface with a recurrent Ricci operator in Euclidean space must be totally umbilical, provided its dimension is at least four. Finally, we demonstrate that a biharmonic hypersurface in Euclidean space with a recurrent semi-symmetric tensor operator must be minimal. These findings extend and refine several existing results. Additionally, we examine biharmonic hypersurfaces in Euclidean space characterized by recurrent harmonic and anti-symmetric tensor operators. As a consequence, we show that no such hypersurfaces exist in Euclidean space. These results generalize and improve upon known theorems. The primary tools employed in this study include the Gauss and Codazzi equations, along with the concepts of biharmonic and harmonic tensors.

When an adhesive tape is peeled, the sound it generates is often described as crackling noise. This paper examines the acoustic emission from a Scotch tape being pulled at a constant speed. The resulting sound spectrum exhibits a $1/f$-like characteristic, and the acoustic power follows a power-law dependence on the pulling velocity. These acoustic signals display intermittent bursts, which are analyzed using a combination of wavelet analysis and a first-order return map. The findings indicate that the acoustic bursts arise from a period-doubling cascade, suggesting the existence of an underlying deterministic chaotic process. This chaotic behavior is linked to the stick-slip dynamics of the tape. These results provide a detailed description of the acoustic emission during the peeling of an adhesive tape, offering insights into the stick-slip dynamics of the tape and the associated acoustic bursts. The methodology presented here can be applied to other systems exhibiting stick-slip dynamics, such as earthquakes, landslides, and tectonic plate movements. Additionally, the approach may be useful for analyzing acoustic emissions from other adhesive tapes, including duct tapes and masking tapes. In 1928, F. Menger introduced the concept of an abstract angle space, a structure designed to formalize the notion of angle between lines within a metric space. He investigated the conditions under which such a space could be embedded into a Euclidean space. In 1973, J. Tits posed the question of whether an abstract angle space could be embedded into a spherical building. In 1999, N. J. Wormald demonstrated that if an abstract angle space satisfies a specific regularity condition, then Tits' query is equivalent to asking whether the space can be embedded into a Euclidean space. This paper resolves two longstanding issues originally raised by Menger regarding abstract angle spaces. First, we establish that if an abstract angle space is embeddable into a Euclidean space, it must satisfy a regularity condition. Second, we prove that for a regular abstract angle space, the embeddability into a Euclidean space is equivalent to the embeddability into a spherical building. These findings confirm that Wormald's equivalence holds universally for all regular abstract angle spaces. Additionally, we provide a concise proof of the fact that embeddability into a Euclidean space is equivalent to embeddability into a Hilbert space for regular abstract angle spaces. Point cloud models have recently gained traction for their capacity to learn representations of 3D scenes, with applications ranging from classification to recognition tasks. These models are typically trained using a one-hot encoding scheme for transformations, such as rotations, which creates a sparse distribution. This sparsity causes the model to overfit to the specific training transformations, resulting in poor generalization to unseen transformations. To address this, we introduce TPC, a transformation-specific smoothing method that replaces the one-hot encoding with a softmax distribution. We hypothesize that this approach enables the model to learn representations invariant to transformations. Our experiments demonstrate that TPC significantly outperforms existing methods on classification and recognition tasks, particularly when dealing with unseen transformations. Furthermore, we show that TPC enhances the performance of other smoothing techniques, such as data-specific smoothing. The source code for TPC is available at https://github.com/tpc-3d/tpc.

Testing serves as a vital technique for ensuring the correctness of software systems. This paper introduces a geometric framework for program testing, offering a unified approach to various testing methods. We demonstrate that traditional testing strategies, including random, symbolic, and concolic testing, can be understood as specific instances of a broader geometric framework. Furthermore, we introduce a novel testing method grounded in this framework and validate its effectiveness through experiments. These results indicate that our new method surpasses conventional techniques in both coverage and performance. Finally, we discuss how this geometric framework can be leveraged to develop automated testing strategies. The proposed framework is implemented within the GeoTest tool, which is available at https://github.com/GeoTest/GeoTest.

Fiber-reinforced composites are increasingly utilized in structural health monitoring (SHM) to detect and characterize damage. While electrical impedance tomography (EIT) is a promising technique for imaging damage in self-sensing composites, it has historically been limited to binary detection, identifying only the presence or absence of damage. This study introduces a novel approach to precisely locate and quantify damage in self-sensing composite laminates using EIT combined with a genetic algorithm (GA). The methodology involves training a GA to optimize a damage shape function, which is then integrated into an electrical conductivity tensor model to predict the composite's electrical conductivity. These predictions are compared against conductivity data derived from EIT measurements. The results demonstrate that the GA can accurately determine both the location and size of damage, with a maximum error of 1.2 mm for location and 0.0001 for size. Furthermore, the study confirms that the precision of damage size estimation is directly influenced by the accuracy of the location prediction. This research provides a new framework for precisely locating and sizing damage in self-sensing composites, offering a significant advancement over traditional binary detection methods. The proposed technique is applicable to various self-sensing materials, including carbon fiber-reinforced polymers and graphene/polymer composites, and could be valuable for optimizing damage repair processes. The detailed methodology for integrating EIT and the GA to achieve precise damage shape characterization is outlined in the following sections. First, the electrical conductivity tensor model is described, followed by the specific implementation of the GA for damage shape optimization. Finally, the results of this integrated approach are presented.

This study examines the geometric significance of tensor components within a Euclidean space, with a specific focus on the components of the metric tensor. We demonstrate that the components of the metric tensor are not merely abstract elements of a tensor but possess intrinsic geometric meaning, serving as the fundamental basis for defining all other geometric quantities. Furthermore, we establish that the components of any tensor can be expressed as a function of the metric tensor components and a set of geometric quantities that are independent of the metric. These findings suggest that the components of the metric tensor carry the same geometric significance as the components of the basis vectors themselves. Consequently, the components of any tensor can be defined as a function of the components of the basis vectors and a set of geometric quantities independent of the basis vectors. This approach offers a novel perspective on the geometric interpretation of tensor components, potentially beneficial for both theoretical and practical applications. Ultimately, we conclude that the components of the metric tensor are the essential geometric quantities required to define the components of any tensor. These results are derived entirely from the axioms of Euclidean geometry, without relying on the concept of a tensor. The paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the notation and definitions of geometric quantities used throughout the work. Section 3 defines the components of the metric tensor and establishes their geometric significance. Section 4 derives the components of an arbitrary tensor as a function of the metric tensor components and a set of geometric quantities independent of the metric. Finally, Section 5 summarizes the main conclusions.

This paper examines the splittings of right-angled Artin groups (RAAGs) associated with specific graphs. We demonstrate that for a finite collection of graphs $\Gamma_1, \dots, \Gamma_n$ defined on the same vertex set $V$, the corresponding RAAGs $A(\Gamma_1), \dots, A(\Gamma_n)$ admit non-trivial splittings over finite subgroups if and only if the graphs $\Gamma_1, \dots, \Gamma_n$ share a common induced subgraph $\Gamma$ with at least two vertices that does not admit a non-trivial acyclic orientation. As a consequence, we establish that the commutator subgroup of a non-trivial RAAG $A(\Gamma)$ is free precisely when $\Gamma$ contains no induced subgraph with two vertices lacking a non-trivial acyclic orientation. Iterative matrix inversion techniques, such as the Jacobi and Newton methods, are valuable for accelerating matrix inversion in applications where direct inversion is impractical due to memory constraints or computational cost. These methods are particularly beneficial for large-scale matrix operations in deep learning, computer vision, and natural language processing. This paper introduces a novel approach to accelerate iterative matrix inversion by generalizing the Newton method to higher orders, resulting in a faster algorithm. We demonstrate that this generalized method converges more rapidly than the Newton method and other existing iterative approaches. Furthermore, we introduce a new technique to optimize the computational complexity of the generalized higher-order method, achieving a faster algorithm than the generalized approach itself. Our proposed algorithm is suitable for GPU acceleration and can be implemented with a computational complexity of $O(n^{1.58})$. Experimental results show that our algorithm outperforms the Newton method and other iterative methods in terms of speed. Additionally, we provide a generalized higher-order method that surpasses the computational complexity of the CULA library's matrix inversion algorithm. The proposed algorithm is applicable to any square matrix, regardless of size. To validate our findings, we conducted experiments on a GPU with 11 GB of memory using matrices of various dimensions. The results confirm that our algorithm exceeds the performance of the Newton method and other iterative methods, and it surpasses the CULA library's inversion algorithm for matrices up to 4096 $\times$ 4096. For larger matrices, our algorithm offers a significant speed advantage over the CULA library. These results indicate that our generalized higher-order method is suitable for accelerating matrix inversion in large-scale deep learning tasks. Contextual bandits represent a significant area of research in online learning, with numerous studies focusing on scenarios where agents lack full access to contextual information. In such cases, agents must rely on a centralized server to retrieve contextual details. This paper investigates the contextual linear bandit problem within a distributed framework where agents operate without knowledge of the context. We introduce a novel algorithm that achieves a regret bound of $O(d\sqrt{T}\log T)$, where $d$ denotes the dimension of the linear model and $T$ represents the time horizon. This result represents the first logarithmic regret bound for contextual linear bandits in a distributed setting where agents are unaware of the context. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(d\sqrt{T})$ for this problem. Our findings indicate that the proposed algorithm is nearly optimal regarding the dependence on $d$ and $T$. To reach these conclusions, we developed a new proof technique for the upper bound that avoids the traditional reduction to a multi-armed bandit problem, which typically introduces a $\sqrt{N}$ factor (with $N$ being the number of actions). Additionally, we derived a lower bound for the distributed contextual linear bandit problem where agents possess partial context information. This lower bound demonstrates that the regret increases with the number of missing context dimensions, suggesting that the performance of contextual linear bandits is sensitive to the completeness of contextual data. Finally, we conducted extensive simulations to validate our theoretical results. The proposed algorithm is applicable to various domains, including sensor networks, where sensor nodes may not have direct access to contextual information. For instance, in a smart grid, sensor nodes might not know the current time of day but can still learn optimal actions, such as adjusting power levels, to maximize rewards. Similarly, in a sensor network monitoring a forest fire, nodes may not know the fire's location but can learn the best actions to take, such as deploying drones to specific areas, to maximize rewards. These scenarios illustrate that agents do not necessarily need to know the context to learn optimal actions. The proposed algorithm is particularly valuable in situations where agents cannot access contextual information due to privacy concerns or limited resources. For example, in a sensor network monitoring a forest fire, nodes may not want to share the fire's location with a central server due to privacy issues. In such cases, the proposed algorithm enables nodes to learn optimal actions without requiring access to contextual information. Overall, this work offers a significant advancement in the field of contextual bandits, providing a new algorithm that allows agents to learn optimal actions

We investigate the vertical shear instability (VSI) in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, focusing on how dust evolution influences the instability's growth rate. Our findings indicate that the VSI growth rate is highly sensitive to the dust settling timescale. Specifically, the instability is suppressed when the dust settling timescale is short, a condition that aligns with the rapid settling of large dust particles. Conversely, the growth rate increases as the dust settling timescale lengthens, which corresponds to the settling of smaller particles. These results suggest that dust evolution can significantly alter the VSI growth rate in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Consequently, the VSI may not be an effective mechanism for generating turbulence in these areas if dust evolution is taken into account. This conclusion holds even when considering the effects of gas cooling and the transition from molecular to atomic hydrogen. These insights offer valuable guidance for future research on the origins of gas and dust accretion in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. Additionally, our results imply that the VSI growth rate is likely overestimated in current literature, which has assumed a constant dust-to-gas ratio. This overestimation could lead to an inflated prediction of the viscous timescale, potentially causing a mismatch between theoretical models and observational data regarding the accretion rate in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks. To address this discrepancy, we propose that dust evolution in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks may be more rapid than previously thought. This hypothesis could help reconcile the difference between the viscous timescale derived from the accretion rate and the viscous timescale calculated using a standard dust-to-gas ratio. Ultimately, our findings suggest that dust evolution in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks may be faster than anticipated, a conclusion that warrants further investigation. The results presented here are derived from a linear stability analysis. To fully understand the impact of dust evolution on the VSI in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, future work should focus on nonlinear stability analyses and numerical simulations. Such efforts will be essential for determining whether the VSI can effectively drive turbulence in these disk regions. This study introduces a novel backdoor attack designed to evade detection by existing methods, termed the dynamic global average pooling (DGAP) backdoor. Unlike conventional static backdoors that rely on fixed trigger patterns, the DGAP backdoor operates without any visible trigger. Instead, it activates only when specific image content is present, enabling a more covert and potent form of poisoning. The core mechanism involves embedding a hidden trigger within the image content itself, which is then amplified by a dynamic global average pooling layer. This layer selectively extracts the embedded trigger and maps it to a target class. We demonstrate that this approach is effective for various poisoning strategies, including feature-based, data-dependent, and feature-dependent backdoors. Furthermore, we show that the DGAP backdoor can bypass detection by state-of-the-art methods, such as the Tricky Filter (TF) detector. To validate these claims, we conducted experiments on the MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CelebA datasets. Results indicate that the DGAP backdoor is both more potent and harder to detect than traditional static backdoors. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the DGAP's effectiveness across different poisoning strategies and its ability to evade various detection techniques. Finally, we introduce a new method to counteract the DGAP backdoor, which we also evaluate for efficacy. The source code for this work is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi0909/DynamicBackdoor.

Long short-term memory (LSTM) networks are integral to numerous video recognition systems, yet their substantial computational and memory demands hinder deployment on resource-constrained devices. This study introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design framework for energy-efficient LSTMs tailored to video recognition tasks. First, we introduce a novel hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition (HTD) method to compress LSTMs, which, when combined with a specific quantization strategy, yields a highly compact model. These findings confirm that the HTD-based LSTM offers a superior balance of accuracy and energy efficiency compared to traditional LSTMs and other tensor decomposition techniques. Bayes factors serve as a standard metric for comparing models, yet their practical application is complicated by the sensitivity of Bayesians to prior distributions. This sensitivity often renders Bayes factors difficult to compute for complex models, particularly when utilizing the conventional Savage-Dickey method. To address these challenges, we introduce a workflow that leverages the generalized Savage-Dickey approach alongside the Cauchy prior mass method. We demonstrate the utility of this workflow through a case study involving the comparison of two models for the cosmic microwave background (CMB) power spectrum. The analysis reveals that the optimal model selection depends on the specific CMB frequency range under consideration. Discourse markers (DMs) are linguistic elements that signal relationships between sentences, such as contrast, causality, or temporal sequence. While numerous studies have investigated the automatic classification of DMs, there has been limited exploration into the semantic analysis of the discourse relations they express. This paper introduces a dataset of 10,000 English sentences annotated with both the specific DM and the corresponding discourse relation, derived from the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB). We also present a taxonomy of 17 discourse relations, which expands upon the standard three-level taxonomy of the PDTB. Leveraging this dataset, we developed a neural network model capable of predicting the discourse relation based on the DM and its surrounding context. Our results indicate that the model can accurately identify the discourse relation even when the DM is replaced with a generic placeholder. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the model can be trained to predict the appropriate DM for a given discourse relation and context. These findings suggest that the semantic meaning of a DM is largely determined by the discourse relation it signals and the contextual information. To facilitate further research, we have made the dataset and all associated code publicly available at https://github.com/linguistics-group/UDM.

We demonstrate that the decomposition of OPE blocks into conformal partial waves for spinning operators is not unique. Finally, we show that the conformal partial wave for a spinning OPE block can be expressed as a linear combination of conformal partial waves for OPE blocks involving lower-dimensional operators. These findings suggest that the conformal partial wave for a spinning OPE block is not a fundamental object. Consequently, the conformal partial wave for a spinning OPE block cannot be used to derive the conformal block for a spinning OPE, as previously claimed in the literature. We also provide a proof of this assertion. Additionally, we derive the explicit form of the conformal partial wave for a spinning OPE block. As a byproduct, we derive the explicit form of the conformal partial wave for a non-spinning OPE block. These results may have significant implications for the AdS$_{3}$/CFT$_{2}$ correspondence. We present a relativistic first principles approach for investigating Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states in magnetic impurities and impurity pairs situated on superconducting surfaces. Skin cancer detection is a significant challenge in the medical field, with the identification of malignant lesions being a critical task. We evaluated our framework using the ISIC 2018 dataset, which contains 10,000 images across five categories.
